review.reason: Read experiments, analysis, and model limits; teaches why bulk flow can conceal particle dynamics.

item.title: Multiscale transitional flow in anisotropic nanoparticle suspensions revealed by time-resolved X-ray scatter microscopy
item.headline: Tiny particles do not always follow a liquid's larger waves
item.summary: Graphene-oxide platelets tracked large vortex waves; cellulose rods showed faster orientation changes. These laboratory suspensions do not establish a rule for every complex fluid.

evidence.question: Does particle alignment track bulk flow?
evidence.method: Polarized-light imaging and X-ray scattering in suspensions between rotating-inner and stationary-outer cylinders.
evidence.limitations: Measurements capture averaged orientation projections, not individual trajectories.

explainer.finding: The rods' faster signal correlated with circulation within vortices rather than their larger waving motion.
explainer.method: Researchers compared frequency patterns from optical videos and X-ray measurements at 14 positions.
explainer.meaning: For example, watching waves in a cellulose suspension would miss its rods' faster reorientation.
explainer.limits: A simple model loses the signal when realistic rotational diffusion is included. Particle interactions may sustain it, but the mechanism remains unresolved.
